title: The ships from Manila
learnerQuestion: What did the ships from Manila bring to New Spain around 1602, who wanted the trade stopped, and why was it not stopped?
sensitiveContentNotice: One part of this Story, "The people on the ship", describes people held as slaves and carried across the Pacific, a woman detained at the port of Acapulco, and the great fall in the Indigenous population of Central Mexico.

paragraphs.text: This view is of 1602. The fullest account we have of a crossing in these years is of a ship that landed the year after.
On 19 December 1603 a ship from Manila made the port of Acapulco.
Acapulco was in New Spain, the kingdom the king of Spain ruled through a viceroy, his governor, in Mexico City.
One of those aboard was a judge, Antonio de Morga, on his way to a post in Mexico City. The account is his.
The ship had left the Philippines in July. Off the coast it met storms, and lightning killed three men.
Morga wrote afterwards that the crossing usually took five months, and often six or more, with no port touched on the way.
He called Acapulco a good, sheltered port, eighty leagues from Mexico City, with a chief magistrate, many Spanish residents and a royal treasury.
Of what he saw when he stepped ashore, his book says nothing.
What ships like his carried, how it was paid for, and who wanted the trade stopped, is the Story.
The ships carried Chinese goods. They reached New Spain by way of Manila, in the Philippines, which the king of Spain also held. How they came to Manila is another Story.
By the 1590s Chinese goods were on sale in the shops and streets of Mexico City.
A historian of the trade writes that a shopkeeper who died in 1592 had sold silk cloth and stockings 'all from China'.
In 1598 a man asked the city council for leave to open what his request calls 'a Chinese shop', in the street of the cloth sellers.
Tailors ordered silk from Manila themselves.
The papers of a tailor who died in 1591, Manuel Tinoco, record his and another tailor's agreements with a merchant who traded in Manila for them.
A craftswoman, Isabel Villalobos, who also died in 1591, had silk sent to her from the Philippines.
In 1604 a poem in praise of the city was printed there, Bernardo de Balbuena's *Grandeza Mexicana*.
It lists what the city gathered from the world: from the Philippines 'the cream', from Macao 'the most precious', from 'great China, coloured silks'. Our translation from the Spanish.
Macao was a Portuguese town on the coast of China, and has a Story of its own.
The poem is a poet praising his city to a patron. It shows what a resident boasted of, not what anyone counted.

The imports had a cost. The historian José Luis Gasch-Tomás writes that they contributed to a sharp fall in New Spain's own silk production by 1600, and that Puebla, the kingdom's main textile town, was forced to shift from silk to wool. No silk raiser or weaver speaks in any Source we have read.
The goods came by this route. The king's ships left the Philippines from late June, and the crossing to Acapulco usually took five months and often six or more.
At Acapulco the king's officers took a freight charge and a duty.
Morga gives the duty as ten per cent. A historian who went through the treasury accounts finds five.
From Acapulco, historians say, the goods went up to Mexico City by mule.
One reports that in 1592 the viceroy had the track made into a mule road, as the trade grew.
Morga gives the distance as eighty leagues. A modern historian puts the road at about 600 kilometres.
No Source we have read describes a cargo on that road in 1602.
Silver paid for the goods. The law let 500,000 pesos in coin go back to Manila each year.
Historians explain the trade by price. Silver, one of them writes, bought more in Asia than in Europe, and Chinese cloth cost far less in New Spain than what the yearly fleets brought from Spain.
Not all of it stayed. In 1603 the king wrote that Chinese goods went on to Peru, though that was forbidden.
What went on to Seville, in Spain, a historian of the trade writes, was nearly all raw silk; New Spain kept the woven cloth.
The ships carried people as well as goods.
In 1597 the king wrote to his officers at Manila and in Mexico City that passengers boarded with people held as slaves, whom his letter described as Black and also 'from places like Japan'.
He set a number each official might take: six for a departing governor, four for a judge, two for others.
In 1602 or 1603 officials at Acapulco held a woman named Gracia. The record calls her a *china* slave.
The Spanish records used *chinos*, and for a woman *china*, for people brought across the Pacific, whatever land they came from. We use these words only when quoting a record.
She had been sent without the licence the law required of anyone bringing a person held as a slave.
The man who claimed her, Pedro de Vega, came down from Mexico City to pay the duty. The officials would not release her, and he needed an order from the viceroy.
Tatiana Seijas, the historian who found the case, dates it to 1602; the paper she cites is of 1603.
The record is about who owned her. It does not say where she came from, or what became of her.
The port's books record very few of the people carried: seven for 1600 to 1603.
The head accountant of the treasury in Mexico City said that more than two hundred Black people had been landed at Acapulco in those same years.
Neither is a count of everyone carried. The gap between them is what the records show.
One man's account survives.
In 1607 Gregorio Moreno petitioned the government at Seville. The record has him call himself 'an Indian of the Chinese nation from the Philippine islands', in the records' way of naming people.

It names an owner, don Lope de Ulloa. Moreno said he had been taken from his land and his parents' home, and carried to Mexico, to Peru, back to Mexico and then to Spain: 'more than 4,500 leagues'. He was now, he said, 'helpless in a distant land'.
The king granted him money for the journey home. Seijas adds that it proved difficult for him to collect. We do not know whether he got home.
His account reaches us through a petition, and in a historian's English.

Seijas gathered records of 598 enslaved people brought across the Pacific, over more than a century. The work of 182 of them in Mexico City is known: 104 were personal servants and 42 worked in textile mills.
The city wanted workers, and Seijas gives a reason. The collapse of the Indigenous population, she writes, transformed the labour system in Mexico.

That population had fallen very greatly in the century before 1602. A reference history of 2006 says most scholars count diseases brought from the Old World as a significant factor in the fall of American populations.
How great the fall was is not agreed. The best-known estimate, and the same history's caution about it, are on this sentence's Claim.

In 1601 the king ruled that Indigenous people, as free vassals, were not to work in the textile mills. In December 1602 the viceroy gave Mexico City's mill owners four months to buy enslaved Black workers and to send the Indigenous workers away.
The owners protested the cost, and the order was soon relaxed. These were mills of the kind in which some of the people from the ships worked.
Most of the people brought to Manila from abroad and sold there came with Portuguese traders, Seijas writes, from India, from Malacca on the Malay coast, from Macao and from other ports.
In 1584 and 1586 the high court at Manila reported that the Portuguese paid no duty on the people they brought from India and Macao, 'even for those sent to New Spain'.
The Macao Story tells of people carried to Macao.

beats.sensitiveNotice: This part describes people held as slaves and carried from Manila to New Spain, and a woman detained at Acapulco in 1602 or 1603. It tells of the deaths of very many Indigenous people in the century before. It quotes words the Spanish records used.

paragraphs.text: The king had set limits.
Goods worth 250,000 pesos a year might come from the Philippines to New Spain in two ships, and 500,000 pesos in coin might go back. Historians date these terms to 1593.
Only residents of the Philippines were to trade.
That shut out the merchants of Mexico City. They had a guild of their own, the *consulado*, licensed by the king in 1592 and set up in 1594.
The merchants traded all the same.

A historian who read the guild's tax lists for goods landed at Acapulco in 1595 and 1596 found 437 persons who had loaded goods worth a little over 580,000 pesos. The lists, as she reports them, do not say whether that is one year's goods or two.
Thirty of them were guild members, and seventy-eight people paid the tax on behalf of others. She reads that as merchants shipping under other people's names.

One way round the rule was a partner in Manila. A historian reports that in 1593, the year the limits were announced, the guild merchant Diego Rodríguez de Torres formed a company with Lorenzo de Figueroa, who went to live in Manila to buy goods and send them to Mexico City.
Officials at the ports, another historian writes, declined to open the cargo boxes.
In September 1603 the king himself wrote that the limits had been much exceeded.
The city council of Mexico City was a different body from the merchants' guild, and in 1602 it did not want what the merchants wanted.
On 6 May 1602 it told its agent at the king's court in Spain to put one matter to the king before all others.
Three million, it said, left New Spain for the Philippines every year, and more than twelve million in the past five years. The minute names no coin; historians read it as pesos.
In those five years, it said, the city had not had goods worth six hundred thousand pesos in return.
It gave its reason. Goods from Castile, in Spain, had no sale in the city, and many residents and merchants were ruined.
Unless 'this door' was shut altogether, it wrote, it would be the ruin of Castile and of New Spain. Our translation from the Spanish. It was a plea, not a count.
The merchants of Seville, whose fleets carried Spain's goods to America, had asked the king for the same thing.

The king asked the Cardinal-Archbishop of Seville. He answered on 28 October 1603 that, of five causes for the decline of Spain's trade with its American lands, the Philippine trade was the most harmful.
He did not ask for the trade to be closed. He feared the Philippines would be abandoned and the preaching there would end.
But he warned of a second danger: if those lands could live without Spain's goods, Spain could not be sure of keeping them. Our translation from the Spanish.

How much silver was it? In 1603 the king wrote that, by the letters of his viceroys and governors, more than two million in silver and coin was carried away each year, most of it, in his words, 'to the kingdoms of infidels'. Our translation from the Spanish.
Neither his figure nor the council's is a count.
The viceroys in Mexico City, a historian reports, told the king the limits could not be enforced, and advised taxing the trade more heavily in place of restricting it.

On 31 December 1604 the king issued new decrees. They kept the limits of 1593 and moved much of the running of the ships to Manila. Their preamble said each ship carried more than two million in coin declared to his officers 'with the knowledge and leave of my viceroys', besides what went in secret. Our translation from the Spanish.

So why was the trade not stopped? The Cardinal feared losing the Philippines, and the viceroys said the limits could not be kept. Historians add that the pull was strong: the goods were cheap and the silver was there. That last is their explanation, not a record.

**Not yet researched.** This Story stops at the end of 1604, with the king's new decrees. What the trade became after them, what the loss of silver did inside New Spain, where the goods went in Peru, and what Indigenous people of the city and the valley made of any of it have not been researched, so none is offered as a researched path. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.
